problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt[3]{y+1}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36.$

activity_context.topic_title: Line Integrals of Scalar Functions Over Circles

feedback.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed from the point $(0,-4)$ to the point $(4,0)$ in the fourth quadrant?
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066920/assets/0baaafbe9846ccef2c06a3b1a86eccac394344afc2dfd94bba2907ebb1cf2362.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot 4\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
